issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: 'Talking about the future' is a weak and atypical trigger for a life-threatening accident in this profile, and it lacks a clear clinical link to the rest of the selected memory, threat, and appraisal items. The other triggers are interpersonal/victim-related, but this item suggests a different theme that is not supported elsewhere.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'Checking if someone is following me' implies pursuit/interpersonal threat. In a life-threatening accident profile, this is hard to reconcile with the rest of the report, which otherwise reflects generalized danger, hypervigilance, and trauma-memory disturbance rather than a specific persecutory/following threat.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: For a 58-year-old fisherman with a life-threatening accident, 'Reminders of victims' implies exposure to multiple casualties or dead/injured others. That is not impossible, but it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise reads like a personal survival-focused accident trauma rather than a mass-casualty/witnessing-victims presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by disorganized, present-tense reliving ('Cannot Find Words', 'Feels Present Not Past'), which fits severe PTSD, but 'intense rage' on recall points to a qualitatively different emotional tone that is not supported elsewhere by the triggers, threat, or appraisals. With no corroborating anger/blame themes, this item stands out as internally and cross-node incongruent.

vignette:
Anand, a 58-year-old fisherman, had lived his life by the rhythms of the tide. For the decade since his wife passed, his days were a quiet testament to routine: the pre-dawn chill on the docks, the familiar weight of the nets, the easy camaraderie with men he’d known for forty years. The sea was his constant, and his small home was his sanctuary. Six months ago, that constancy was shattered on a winding coastal road. A pickup truck, moving too fast on a wet curve, crossed the center line. Anand remembers the high-pitched screech of his own tires, a sound that seemed to stretch for an eternity before the world became a chaos of shattered glass and the violent, wrenching force of impact. In the awful silence that followed, he saw the other driver, a young man, climb out of his cab, looking dazed but otherwise fine. It was the man’s placid, almost unconcerned expression that lodged itself in Anand’s mind as he sat pinned in his seat, a searing pain in his chest making it impossible to draw a full breath.

In the weeks that followed, the world began to reconfigure itself around that moment. The trauma was not a memory he could place in the past; it was a living thing. Seeing a minor fender-bender in the market parking lot or even an image of a crash on the news would plunge him back into the driver's seat, the terror as immediate and overwhelming as it was that day. The memory feels like it is happening right now, not something that is over, and it brings with it the same gut-wrenching certainty that he is about to die. This visceral re-experiencing has poisoned his perceptions. The memory of his own body failing him—the trapped feeling, the stolen breath—has convinced him that he can no longer trust it to keep him safe. The recollection of the other driver’s detached calm has hardened into a deep, pervasive belief that people are not what they seem, that a benign exterior can hide a catastrophic threat.

These convictions have become the lens through which Anand now views the world. Because he believes his body is unreliable and that others are fundamentally untrustworthy, he lives in a state of constant, exhausting vigilance. He feels on guard even inside his own home, the familiar creaks of the floorboards now sounding like an intruder’s footsteps. Out on the docks or in the market, he finds himself constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of danger, his head on a swivel, unable to relax. This persistent sense of danger seems to hold the accident close to the surface of his mind, as if his brain needs to keep the details ready in case of another sudden impact. This perpetual sense of threat has, in turn, warped his sense of self. The exhaustion from being constantly on alert feels like further proof of his body’s weakness, reinforcing his negative appraisals. He feels like a stranger in his own skin; the capable, steady man he once was has been replaced by this frightened, fragile version, and he no longer knows himself.

This cycle now feeds itself relentlessly. The state of hypervigilance makes him exquisitely sensitive to anything that reminds him of the accident. The unusual silence that falls over the docks just before the morning rush, a quiet he once found peaceful, now feels menacing, mirroring the silence after the impact and yanking the memory back to the forefront of his mind. The intrusive memory, in turn, makes him even more reactive to his triggers; after a flashback, he is more likely to flinch at the sound of screeching tires or to feel a jolt of panic when a stranger approaches him. His belief that he is fundamentally and permanently changed often leads him to ruminate on the accident, the moment he feels his old self was destroyed, which only serves to call up the memory in all its terrifying detail.

His life has shrunk as a result. His work, once his anchor, is now an ordeal. He has to interact with strangers to sell his catch, but each new face now feels like a potential threat, and the simple act of making conversation sends a spike of adrenaline through him. This interaction confirms his belief that people are dangerous, and he often finds himself unable to find the right words, his mind going blank. He has started asking his nephew to manage the stall, retreating to the solitude of his boat where he feels safer, though even there, the quiet can turn against him. A few weeks ago, a well-meaning friend tried to connect with him over their shared experience as widowers. The talk about losing a loved one sent Anand into a spiral, the memory of the crash merging with a profound, overwhelming grief for his wife.

It was this moment that finally brought him to seek help. He felt he had lost not only his sense of safety but his very identity. The man his wife had loved—the strong, quiet fisherman content with his life—was gone, replaced by a man who scans every face for danger and fears the silence of his own home. Anand’s hope for therapy is not grand; it is a desperate wish to quiet the ceaseless internal alarm and to once again feel like he knows the person he sees in the mirror.
